articles.description: This live blog is now closed. Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes Sign up to the Breaking News US email Nvidia ’s shares have surged by 31% at the start of trading following the news. The S+P 500 jumped 4.5% and is recovering nearly half of its brutal losses from last week, which was one of its worst since the 2008 financial crisis. Rallies for AI stocks had the Nasdaq composite up a market-leading 6.5%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 1,117 points. Here’s Trump ’s full social media post, in which he also called Jensen Huang “a Great Patriot and National Treasure”. The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south. Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. articles.title: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child
articles.description: Rockstar Games’ brilliant 18-rated criminal caper is stuffed with sex, drugs and violence. It is the most explicit game I’ve ever played – and it really is not for kids I am haunted still by an interaction I had at my stepson’s ninth birthday party in 2014, where one of the kids asked if I could put on Grand Theft Auto V for them all. “I have it at home!”, he said, giving me the puppy-dog eyes. Mentally replaying that game in my head, flashing back to the many scenes involving such things as smoking meth, over-the-top gratuitous violence and grubby sex in one character’s trailer, I said “ no way” . Later I gently mentioned to the kid’s mother that GTA V was an 18-rated game and really wasn’t suitable for kids. “Oh, but he’s really good at these games,” she told me. She was genuinely shocked to learn that an 18-rating on a video game was a flag for adult content, rather than an indication of its difficulty. Grand Theft Auto VI is released this week. It is an incredible creative and technical feat, conjuring a realistic-looking and exhaustively detailed virtual Florida filled with every kind of filth and criminality you could imagine. It is brilliant, entertainingly observed and even sometimes unexpectedly touching, largely thanks to a central love story between the player couple , Jason and Lucia. It is lewd, violent and frequently hilarious. It is also absolutely full of stuff that I really would not want my 10 and seven-year-old boys to see or hear. I have never played a game that has more thoroughly earned its 18 rating. Continue reading...

The trailer for the video game, which returns players to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, attracted more than 90m views in 24 hours when it was released in December 2023. articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. Continue reading...

articles.description: Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange. The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. articles.title: UK net migration falls to 77,000, lowest since 1997 excluding Covid pandemic – UK politics live
articles.description: Net migration fell in the year ending June 2026, according to the Office for National Statistics The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson, Paul Kohler . Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero. Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services. The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level. British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour’s high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high. British families are left to pay for it with lower wages, longer waits for a GP appointment and homes they cannot afford. Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society. Continue reading...

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, despite concerns over his conduct and the supply of AI chips to China, may show that AI – and Huang himself – are ‘too big to fail’. That phrase was on everyone’s lips almost 20 years ago when the Global Financial Crisis struck, and several major banks were bailed out. Given Nvidia’s pivotal role in the AI capex rollout, the implications of Huang’s reinstatement could be profound. Borrowing from the GFC, are some technology CEOs now so systemically important to the future of AI and US leadership in the latest technology revolution that they cannot be fired? Questions around the scale of financing required and future monetisation remain, and the dependence on Huang for the future success of AI may paradoxically heighten those concerns especially given Anthropic fell despite yesterday’s broad market rally. “We must investigate these actions. articles.subject: Geopolitics

articles.title: EU wants ‘closest possible relationship’ with UK after agreeing Brexit reset deal – live
articles.description: President of European Council says EU ‘remains open to have the closest possible relationship’ with the UK Senior correspondent Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said. Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months , a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China. But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today. This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state. It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink. During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP. “We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.” “Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. articles.description: The Guardian’s UK politics blogger answered readers’ questions These are from my colleague Peter Walker , who was at the Tory event where James Cleverly was named as the party’s candidate for London mayor. Peter posted this before the result was announced. Khan (who may or may not stand a 4th time) has thus far faced a dilettante who decided to campaign on a racist platform (Zack Goldsmith) and two oddballs in Shaun Bailey and then Susan Hall. Not even he can be lucky yet again Interesting that [the Conservatives] did not say how many votes were cast, just the percentage - which perhaps indicates it was not a huge number Cleverly’s speech is mainly an attack on Labour and Khan, which is likely to be a theme for his campaign: “Burnham can’t stand London and Khan stand up to Burnham.” Also a pitch about building houses and cutting crime, and boosting transport. Cleverly says he would “end Khan’s war on motorists”, which is a sign he might lean into the anti-cycling and walking rhetoric which the London Tories have a habit of espousing. Expect talk about LTNs and 20mph zones. In the media Q&A Cleverly is pinned down on whether he backs the Tory party line on wanting to leave the ECHR and opposes net zero. He confirms he does (as he has to). Such things will be ready ammunition for Labour. Cleverly says of Andy Burnham, “His residual behaviour is to be anti-London”. This will very much be a theme of his campaign, it seems. Not sure how resonant a “poor London!” message will be even in London People are leaving London, or not choosing to come here in the first place, businesses, job creators, families leaving London, and by the time of the election in 2028, Khan will have been mayor for 12 years, and those two things are related. The problems London faces are the symptoms. Khan is the cause. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is Spain 'nostalgic' for Franco? Would traditional right PP consider an alliance with far-right Vox?
articles.description: After eight years of socialist-led government, Spain is at a crossroads. Can Pedro Sánchez pull off another electoral comeback, or will the conservative Partido Popular make way for the far right into national government for the first time since the end of Franco's 40-year brutal reign? Just back from Madrid, Richard Werly, Europe correspondent for the Swiss daily Blick, joins Angela Diffley to examine the final days of campaigning and the generational divisions shaping Sunday’s snap elections. The youth are divided between the left and the far-right Vox party. Sánchez, nicknamed the “Teflon politician”, has campaigned heavily on housing and social issues. “We may see an outgoing prime minister performing better than expected,” says Werly.

articles.description: Three party leaders are vying in Spain's general election on Sunday, which leftist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called following a parliamentary setback over housing legislation that underscored the fragility of his minority coalition government. Speaking with FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney, Javier Carbonell, Policy Analyst at the European Policy Centre, says that despite solid economic growth in Spain the population "have suffered a housing crisis and inflation, citizens are still angry with the government and the economic system regardless of macroeconomic data", adding that "in the end citizens are angry with the establishment, in this case it will be Sanchez, but to be honest I think they will be angry at PP and Vox very soon".

articles.title: The unexpected joy hiding in Grand Theft Auto VI’s chaos? A little routine
articles.description: Rockstar’s latest blockbuster makes the everyday business of shopping, working out and taking care of a pet snake as compelling as its shootouts and car chases I knew I’d need many skills during the opening hours of Grand Theft Auto VI, but effective time management was not one of them. From playing the previous five titles in the series (and their many spin-offs), I understood I’d have to master Rockstar’s idiosyncratic approach to car handling. True enough, the vehicles do drive like airbeds tied on top of supermarket trolleys. I also knew I’d need to get to grips with the somewhat tricky aiming and shooting if I was to commit any sort of respectable crime spree. But for the first few hours of playing this staggeringly large and bewildering game, what concerned me most was lead character Jason’s personal routine. Each day, he needs to get up, choose an outfit, complete a workout, feed his pet snake Dolores, and perhaps do some DIY, so that when his girlfriend Lucia gets out of jail she’ll fall for him again – rather than fall through his apartment’s rotten staircase. Meanwhile, his drug-smuggling boss phones every five minutes with new parcels for Jason to pick up or drop off, and his pals Cal and Donnie get into all sorts of cocaine-related hijinks they expect Jason to extricate them from. There are also predatory neighbours to do favours for, and groceries to buy. I’ve seen so many people on social media posting about how they took several days off work to play this game, only to find themselves busier and more productive than ever. On his radio show last week, James O’Brien derided himself for completing, in Jason’s apartment, a simple DIY task that he’s put off for months in his own home. I know where he’s coming from. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard explicitly claimed responsibility for these attacks. The Ministry praised the efficiency, vigilance, and capability of the Bahrain Defense Force in confronting today’s attack and its complete readiness to deter any aggression. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies. Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. articles.title: US Senate ‘permitting bill’ threatens clean water protections to speed up energy projects
articles.description: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act passed the Senate and is now being debated in the House An industry-backed “permitting bill” approved by the US Senate would gut key clean water protections with changes that would do little to speed up the development of major energy projects, advocates warn. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Baaja) passed the Senate 62-33 and is now being debated in the House. The Baaja is a “permitting reform” bill that aims to reduce the time it takes federal agencies to approve major energy and infrastructure projects, like power lines, fossil fuel pipelines, natural gas plants and datacenters . articles.title: Climate scientists urge US lawmakers to vote no on sweeping permitting bill
articles.description: Open letter warns Baaja, intended to expedite energy and infrastructure projects, will cause irreversible climate harm A group of more than 120 climate scientists have urged US lawmakers to not pass contentious legislation to speed up the building of energy projects, datacenters and other infrastructure, amid a growing backlash to the sweeping permitting bill. In an open letter to members of the House of Representatives , the collection of Earth and social sciences researchers expressed “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja) weakens environmental laws, locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse and delivers only minor cuts to planet-heating emissions. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly. articles.title: The Russian army’s secret death toll – podcast
articles.description: Vladimir Putin has always kept the number of soldiers killed in Ukraine a secret, but at one point 720 were dying in 24 hours. Pjotr Sauer reports. Send your comments and questions to tif.questions@theguardian.com Russia has kept the death toll of its soldiers in the Ukraine war a carefully guarded secret. Now documents leaked to the Guardian have revealed its true scale . The Guardian’s Russia affairs correspondent, Pjotr Sauer , tells Helen Pidd what reporters have discovered. articles.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.description: Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted. “Everything was happening at once. I’ll tell you when I get back.” He never made it home. Five weeks later, shortly after turning 29, Bolgov walked about 300 metres from his unit’s command post near the village of Stepove into woodland and shot himself, according to a written account by his commander seen by the Guardian. articles.title: Australian politics live: Government lacks ‘moral authority’ on decarbonisation, Monique Ryan says; eight teens arrested over alleged schoolies assault
articles.description: Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The government will save more than it spends, says Jim Chalmers , but it won’t be a “slash and burn” budget update. Unlike the federal budget, where we get plenty of notice of when it will be handed down, the government only gives us a few days notice for the mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (or Myefo). There’s still a fair bit of work to do to finalise it all, but we’ve made enough progress to be confident that at this stage there will be a modest net save in the budget. We’re not going to slash and burn in the budget where that would impact the payments that people receive or where it would impact some of the more sensitive parts of the economy. But we haven’t focused the savings on just one portfolio. There will be a number of savings in the mid-year update. They will be substantial, as I said. These are serious times. You can see in the quite extraordinary reaction on the stock market just how volatile global markets are right now. I think it’s a bit of a symbol of the quite extraordinary volatility, unpredictability that we’re seeing play out in markets in the AI sector, but more broadly as well. Continue reading...

Negotiators are also split over a proposed global electrification target, carbon capture and the future of UN climate science reports. articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.description: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states. In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent. Continue reading...

articles.title: ICJ ruling on Myanmar genocide: ‘Historic victory for Rohingya, landmark for international justice’
articles.description: Erin Ogunkeye welcomes Reed Brody, Member of the International Commission of Jurists, Human Rights Lawyer and veteran war crimes prosecutor. The International Court of Justice's ruling on Myanmar marks, according to Brody, "a historic victory for the Rohingya, but also a landmark for international justice." He explains how the court assessed evidence of genocidal intent, rejecting Myanmar's justification of its military operations as counterterrorism. He argues that "the existence of an armed conflict or a security objective doesn't exclude genocidal intent," a finding he believes will have "far-reaching implications in future genocide cases," including South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Brody also discusses the Gambia's role in bringing the case and growing challenges to international accountability, warning that "we're in a very dangerous moment."

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group. With five months to go before France's presidential election, Marine Le Pen leads the opinion polls, while Jean-Luc Mélenchon emerges as her most likely second-round opponent. Lecomte says that "the other candidates are basically fighting for the second spot" and that the center and right are "desperately trying to find a way to avoid a second round" between the two. articles.title: Russia's war on Ukraine: 'Americans want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine & Europe'
articles.description: Delano D'Souza is pleased to welcome Grégoire Roos, Director of the Europe and Russia and Eurasia Programmes at Chatham House. As European countries prepare to take part in the next round of Ukraine peace talks, Roos questions whether having five European representatives could weaken their negotiating position. "The other option is to realize that it dilutes the negotiating power of Europe. And I would lean towards that," he says, proposing Finnish President Alexander Stubb as a possible representative. Roos also points to differences between Washington and European governments over negotiations with Russia. While "the Americans do absolutely want to have a deal whatever the cost for both Ukraine and Europe," he argues that European governments have little choice but to maintain pressure on Moscow, which has yet to abandon its "maximalist demands."

articles.title: The best cordless vacuum cleaners for a spotless home: 10 tried and tested favourites
articles.description: Stick vacuums are a convenient alternative to corded designs, but which model wins for overall cleaning prowess? Our expert reveals all • The best robot vacuums • How to make your vacuum last longer Choosing a cordless vacuum is a big decision. Whichever model you go for, you’re likely to use it for years, relying on its ability to suck up dust, crumbs, mud, pet hair and any other dry spillages or sheddings. Choosing the right model can be the difference between an effective cleaner that’s a delight to pull out of the cupboard and a dud that you dread having to unblock, detangle and clean after every use. In this review, I took 18 of the leading cordless vacuum cleaners from a range of manufacturers and at various prices and inflicted the same cleaning tests on each one. That takes all the guesswork out of picking your next cleaner: I can tell you exactly which ones picked up the most mess, and how easy and enjoyable they were to use. Continue reading...

articles.title: Slow internet? The best wifi extenders and mesh systems to boost your home network – tested
articles.description: We put 11 range extenders and mesh systems to the test to find the fastest and most reliable for streaming, gaming and working from home • The best office chairs Fast fibre broadband is fantastic – if the wifi signal reaches the part of your home where you need it. Most of us use the router provided by our broadband provider, often tucked away in a hallway or corner of the lounge. Sadly, these often don’t have the range to cover every room in your home, leaving you high and dry when you’re trying to binge-watch TV or get work done in a distant home office. Wifi extenders and mesh systems can help. Extenders plug in to a mains socket between your location and the router, then pass data backwards and forwards to extend your router’s reach. Mesh systems are even smarter, pairing a secondary router with one or two satellite units, which work together to extend the wifi coverage throughout your home. The mesh system can pass your connection from unit to unit to make sure you’re always getting the best possible link from your device to the internet, wherever you are in your home. Continue reading...

articles.title: At critical juncture, Friedrich Merz finds Germans’ support for Ukraine wavering
articles.description: German chancellor is on difficult terrain, at home and abroad, as he fights to maintain European backing for Kyiv The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is navigating choppy waters both at home and abroad over his insistence that Europe must keep up support – both military and financial – for Ukraine. At a Brussels summit on Thursday, Merz reiterated his view that all EU member states – pointedly, “not 23 or 24” – should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. He has threatened to veto the bloc’s budget unless all countries sign up to the loan, a stance that saw him accused of “classic blackmail” by Robert Fico, the populist prime minister of Slovakia. articles.title: Graham Thorpe’s widow takes legal action against NHS trust after inquest
articles.description: Former England Test cricketer was diagnosed with anxiety and depression before he took his own life in 2024 The wife of Graham Thorpe, the former England cricketer who took his own life, has started legal proceedings against an NHS trust after an inquest identified “failings” in his mental health care. articles.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
articles.description: Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions. They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets. articles.title: French student protests: A 'very bizarre' government response
articles.description: “The government had a very bizarre way of dealing with the student protests,” says Jean-Rémi Girard, a secondary school teacher and union representative in Asnières-sur-Seine. He explains how teachers sought to defuse tensions by listening to students, and respecting their right to protest, while keeping classes running. He recounts a police intervention last October and the case of a student facing trial for defending a classmate, and has the full support of several teachers. Girard questions the government's heavy-handed policing and largely symbolic proposals on class sizes and university admissions. “There wasn't really a negotiation,” he says, also highlighting the number of education workers injured during the protests.

articles.title: Back to Black Friday: 'We are now bombarded with offers throughout the year'
articles.description: Black Friday was once a single day of holiday sales, held the day after Thanksgiving. Then retailers began kicking things off a day early, on Thanksgiving itself. “We are now bombarded with offers throughout the year,” says Hilary Ingham, Professor of Economics and Department Head at Lancaster University, who has no plans to shop this Black Friday. Ingham acknowledges a growing sense of “retail fatigue” but still sees the potential for a peak in sales. Meanwhile, an investigation by The Telegraph suggests that six in ten of the most popular products were actually more expensive than earlier in the year, underscoring the need for consumers to remain vigilant and track prices over time.

articles.title: Three studies link glyphosate to cancer, contradicting claims of Trump EPA
articles.description: Experts say NIH research raises concerns about chemical companies’ influence on US agency’s pesticide division The US government’s top medical research agency has released three new studies linking glyphosate, the world’s most widely used pesticide and an active ingredient in Roundup, to cancer . The National Institutes of Health (NIH) findings contradict a controversial recent Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) conclusion that the weedkiller is not a carcinogen, and deals a blow to the White House, which has been closely allied with Roundup’s producer, Bayer. The NIH’s three papers could have significant political and legal fallout. The EPA is in the process of a court-ordered re-evaluation of glyphosate’s cancer risks. The NIH findings generate new pressure for the EPA to find that the substance is linked to cancer, which would subject it to a modest increase in regulations. Continue reading...

articles.title: It’s the biggest ever month for video games – so why am I playing a title from 2006? | Dominik Diamond
articles.description: While everyone else is giddy over Zelda and GTA, Dominik Diamond finds himself behind the times on a Nintendo Wii I find myself on the wrong side of gaming history this month. I have zero zeitgeist. My takes are as fresh as something found at the rear of the fridge. I haven’t even played Grand Theft Auto VI yet, but we’ll get to that. Worse, all month, the Nintendo sector of the gaming world has been going googly eyed over Zelda. The Ocarina of Time remake seems to have produced more joy than all the puppies in the world. But not for me. I have never liked Zelda. It’s like being a movie reviewer who doesn’t like Disney, or a vegan shark. Continue reading...

articles.title: How years of research built Grand Theft Auto VI’s obsessively detailed world
articles.description: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.” Continue reading...
articles.subject: Science

articles.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
articles.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

articles.title: GTA in Istanbul? Meet the game developers bringing virtual crime chaos to their home cities
articles.description: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. The Times reports that employees at the NSA’s Maryland headquarters are under “code orange” for Thursday day shift, which requires non-essential workers are to stay home unless contacted by their supervisors. A secret, closed-door election: Unlike the public speaker of the House vote, where lawmakers cast ballots on the chamber floor, the Senate leadership contest takes place behind closed doors. Senators vote by secret ballot, and individual votes are not disclosed. The winner only needs a caucus majority: The Democratic leadership race is decided solely by members of the party’s Senate caucus. Now that Democrats are set to have 56 seats in the new year, the winner will need secure 29 votes for the top role. The vote is scheduled for next month: As things stand, the election is set for 1 December . Both incumbent senators and incoming Democratic members will participate, while retiring and outgoing senators will not vote, despite many having publicly weighed in on the race. Republicans choose their leaders separately: Republicans hold their own closed-door leadership elections in both chambers. Earlier this month, House Republicans selected hardliner Jim Jordan as their leader after Mike Johnson opted not to run for minority leader. articles.title: Killer tunes: how Grand Theft Auto conquered the music world
articles.description: Featuring hundreds of songs from the hippest real-world artists, the radio stations in Rockstar’s crime sagas are as hotly anticipated as the storylines. Contributors including Flying Lotus, Wavves and Nite Jewel reflect on the soundtracks’ curation and impact • The exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI • Crime pays: how GTA became a cultural colossus • Ten movies (and one TV show) that inspired GTA A droptop sports car speeds along a highway blaring 90s west coast rap from its booming sound system. Gradually, the asphalt gives way to rural backwaters, and so the sounds of Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas’s local radio also change: less gangster rap and more twangin’ country – the grizzled croon of Merle Haggard and yearning warble of Patsy Cline. The Grand Theft Auto games are massive, stretching across many, many square miles of virtual terrain. Their soundtracks, relayed mostly via in-game radio stations, are manifold. And these two aspects, plus the personal experiences each player brings to the game, mean everyone has a different favourite musical memory from the smash-hit crime series. For acclaimed electronic musician Flying Lotus, it is all the hours he spent cavorting around 2004’s San Andreas that remain special. “It felt like the first time a game saw a different side of culture – black culture,” he says over the phone. “It felt like we were being seen. And with the extent of the music, all the cool California hip-hop, it felt like someone actually cared.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
articles.description: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...
